prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Assess the competitive advantages (economic moat) and pricing power of the publicly listed company "TEXAS INSTRUMENTS INC" (ticker TXN), and list its competitors. Use the most recent information you know. Never invent figures: use null when unsure. Be specific (products, numbers, years).

Reply with ONLY one JSON object, no other text, in exactly this shape:
{
 "name": "official company name", "ticker": "TXN", "industry": "industry in a few words",
 "markets": ["the main product markets it competes in"],
 "mission": {"statement": "the company's own official mission statement, word for word as it publishes it; null if you are not sure of the exact wording (never paraphrase here)",
             "source": "where it is published, e.g. company website or 2025 annual report, or null",
             "plain": "what the mission means, in one short simple sentence"},
 "about": {"plain": "3-4 short sentences explaining what the company does, in simple everyday words a 12-year-old would understand; no jargon",
           "customers": "who buys from it, in one simple sentence",
           "everyday": "one sentence linking it to something ordinary people know or use, or null",
           "money": [ {"part": "business line in simple words", "share": decimal share of sales or null, "plain": "what it sells there, in a few simple words", "tag": "main|new|moonshot"} ]  (its main ways of making money, largest first, up to 6; also include any new business line or one with explosive, moonshot potential even if its sales are still small. tag: "main" = an established line that brings in a large part of sales; "new" = launched or entered in roughly the last 3 years; "moonshot" = could grow many times over or reshape the company, e.g. a new technology or market, even if unproven. Give each line one tag, the one that fits best)},
 "summary": "2-3 plain-English sentences on whether and why it has a competitive advantage",
 "pricingPower": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "specific evidence, e.g. price rises and what happened to volumes"},
 "moats": [ {"source": one of ["Brand and intangible assets","Switching costs","Network effects","Cost advantage and scale","Efficient scale","Counter-positioning","Process power (hard-to-copy know-how)","Cornered resource (exclusive asset or talent)"], "strength": "strong|moderate|weak|none", "evidence": "one or two specific sentences"} ]  (all 8 sources, in that order),
 "customers": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "customer satisfaction and loyalty: retention, NPS, reviews, repeat purchase"},
 "talent": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "ability to attract and keep top talent: employer rankings, reputation, pay"},
 "product": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "is the product best in class? independent benchmarks, awards, ecosystem"},
 "competitors": [ {"name": "company name", "ticker": "main listing ticker (exchange suffix if not US, e.g. 005930.KS) or null if private",
                   "usTicker": "ticker of its US listing or ADR that files reports with the SEC, or null", "overlap": "high|medium|low",
                   "note": "where they compete"} ]  (every significant competitor, most direct first, up to 15; include major private ones with ticker null),
 "estimates": [ {"name": "company name", "fy": "FY2025", "currency": "USD", "revenueUSDm": number, "revenueGrowth3y": decimal, "grossMargin": decimal, "operatingMargin": decimal, "netMargin": decimal} ]
   (approximate latest fiscal-year figures for the company itself and for every listed competitor; decimals, e.g. 0.42; null if unknown),
 "marketShare": [ {"market": "market name", "measure": "revenue|units|shipments|...", "latestYear": "2025", "earlierYear": "2020",
                   "rows": [ {"name": "company name", "latest": decimal or null, "earlier": decimal or null} ] } ]  (up to 3 of its main markets, the company and its main rivals),
 "threats": ["specific things that could weaken its advantage"],
 "ceo": {"name": "current CEO", "founder": true or false, "since": "YYYY", "background": "e.g. electrical engineer, Stanford MBA"},
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence with names, numbers or examples"} }  for EVERY id below:
   "c1": Rule Breaker #1: is it the leader of an important industry that is still emerging and growing fast?
   "c2": Rule Breaker #2: why do customers choose it over rivals (brand, better value, innovation, culture, leadership), and is that advantage hard to copy and likely to last many years?
   "c3": Rule Breaker #5: do ordinary people recognise the name, is it the default leader in its field (like Google, Amazon, NVIDIA, Tesla, Intuitive Surgical, Netflix), and would customers recommend its product?
   "c4": Does it have an inspiring mission it keeps emphasising, with management driven by purpose rather than money? If it spends 10 years doing this, would it matter?
   "c6": What is the general public consensus about the company and its products or services? When people hear the name, what are the first few descriptive words that come to mind? Start the evidence with those words in quotes (e.g. “innovative, premium, reliable”), then say whether that impression is mostly positive.
   "c7": Is its total addressable market large and growing, riding a secular trend (like CRWD, NVDA, TSLA, AMZN)?
   "c8": Does it have room to expand into big new markets: in its name, its technology or its vision?
   "m1": Is the CEO a visionary with a clear picture of the future?
   "m2": Is the CEO a founder (or acting like one): long-term thinking, working extraordinarily hard, pouring heart and soul into building something that outlives them?
   "m4": Does the CEO lead by serving employees and customers?
   "m5": Has the CEO deliberately built a strong, distinctive culture that keeps inventing new products and technologies?
   "m6": Is the CEO deeply hands-on with the product and technology, ideally with an engineering background?
   "m7": Is the CEO a person of great character who cares about something bigger than profit? For successor CEOs: is stewardship aimed at the benefit of humanity?
   "m7b": Has the CEO been invited to give a commencement speech at a top university (Stanford, Harvard, MIT, etc.)? Name it.
   "m8b": Does the CEO have a distinctive, memorable personality (like Elon Musk, Alex Karp, Larry Page)?
   "m9": Has the CEO a strong record of execution and results?
   "m10": Is the CEO and company known for frugality (like Bezos's door desk)?
   "c10": Do its products solve problems for people all over the world, greatly improving the lives of a very large number of people (like NFLX, GOOG, ISRG)?
   "p2": Is what it builds extremely hard to do, and important to the world?
   "f1": Has revenue grown in almost every one of the last five years?
   "f2": Have gross and operating margins risen over the last five years?
   "f3": Is debt low compared with cash and cash flow, with positive shareholders' equity?
   "f4": Have operating income and operating cash flow risen over the last five years?
   "v1": Is its main product clearly the best in its field, with a practical reason an ordinary person can understand for choosing it over every alternative (like NVIDIA over AMD)?
   "v2": Is it widely seen as one of the best companies to work for (culture, mission, reputation, employer rankings)? Cite rankings.
   "c5": Do its products make the world better? If it disappeared overnight, who would notice and miss it, and why?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM of the newest information you used"
}

result.name: Texas Instruments Incorporated
markets: Analog chips (power management and signal chain)
Data center power and signal chips

mission.statement: For decades, we have operated with a passion to create a better world by making electronics more affordable through semiconductors.
mission.source: TI company website, 'Who we are' page (ti.com)
mission.plain: TI wants to make chips that let electronics get cheaper and better so more people can use them.

about.plain: Texas Instruments makes tiny computer chips that sit inside almost every electronic thing. Most of its chips handle electricity and real-world signals, like turning a battery's power into the right amount for a motor or reading a temperature sensor. It also makes small 'brain' chips that control machines, and the famous school calculators. It builds most of its chips in its own factories in Texas and Utah.
about.customers: About 100,000 companies that build cars, factory machines, data centers, phones and gadgets buy its chips, many through TI.com.
about.everyday: The graphing calculator in many school backpacks is a TI-84, and TI chips are inside cars, washing machines, laptops and phone chargers.

money.plain: chips that manage power and read real-world signals (Q2 2026: $4,365M of $5,463M)
microcontrollers and processors that act as small brains in machines and cars (Q2 2026: $788M)
calculators, DLP projector chips and other items (Q2 2026: $310M)

money.part: Data center power and signal chips
money.plain: power and connectivity chips for AI servers, about a tenth of sales in early 2026 and growing about 90% a year
about 1,200 wireless connectivity products from the $7.5B Silicon Labs purchase, expected to close in 1H 2027

result.summary: TI has a durable moat built on scale manufacturing: it is moving nearly all production into its own 300mm fabs in Texas and Utah, which gives it a structural cost advantage in commodity-like analog parts, plus a catalog of 80,000+ products sold to 100,000+ customers, many directly through TI.com. Analog chips are designed into products that ship for 10+ years, so switching costs are real, but pricing power is only moderate and the heavy fab-building cycle cut gross margin from 68.8% (2022) to 57.0% (2025).

pricingPower.evidence: Analog parts are low-cost and sticky once designed in, but TI uses price to win share rather than to maximise margins; pricing was described as flat-to-stable in Q1 2026 despite rising demand, with management only flagging possible increases in 2H 2026 as supply tightens. Gross margin fell from 68.8% in 2022 to 57.0% in 2025 mostly because of fab depreciation and lower volumes, then recovered to 61.4% in Q2 2026 as volumes rose.

moats.evidence: TI is the best-known analog brand among engineers, with a huge library of reference designs, the WEBENCH design tools and TI.com; consumers know it mainly for TI-84 calculators.
Once a TI part is qualified into a car or industrial design it typically ships for 10 years or more, and re-qualifying a rival part costs customers engineering time and risk.
Its broad catalog and engineer community (E2E forums, reference designs) create mild ecosystem effects, but there is no true network effect between users.

TI is the largest analog supplier and is shifting production into owned 300mm fabs (Richardson, Lehi, Sherman), which lowers the cost per chip versus older 200mm wafers, alongside a roughly $50B six-year manufacturing build-out.
The analog market is fragmented across tens of thousands of small, niche parts where it rarely pays a new entrant to compete, though Chinese suppliers are attacking the low end.
While most rivals went fab-light and rely on foundries, TI doubled down on owning internal, geopolitically dependable U.S. capacity, which outsourced rivals cannot easily copy.
Decades of analog process technology and manufacturing know-how, plus direct sales of a large share of revenue through TI.com, are hard to replicate.
Its fabs and CHIPS Act funding support are valuable but not exclusive; no unique resource is locked away from rivals.

customers.evidence: TI serves more than 100,000 customers with 80,000+ products, and long design-in lifecycles in industrial and automotive keep customers buying the same parts for years; no NPS figures are published.

talent.evidence: A respected engineering employer with 33,000+ employees and long-tenured leaders (CEO Haviv Ilan joined in 1999), but it does not rank near the top of major best-employer lists; it appeared at No. 295 on Fortune's 2021 World's Most Admired All-Star list.

product.evidence: TI has the broadest analog and embedded catalog in the industry with strong reliability and long availability; rivals such as Analog Devices lead in some high-performance niches, but TI wins on breadth, supply security and cost.

competitors.name: Analog Devices, Inc.
competitors.note: Closest analog rival in signal chain, power management, industrial and automotive; stronger in high-performance converters.

competitors.name: Infineon Technologies AG
competitors.note: Power semiconductors, automotive MCUs and power management; strong in automotive and data-center power.

competitors.name: STMicroelectronics N.V.
competitors.note: Analog, power and general-purpose microcontrollers (STM32) for industrial and automotive.

competitors.name: NXP Semiconductors N.V.
competitors.note: Automotive and industrial microcontrollers, processors and analog.

competitors.name: Microchip Technology Inc.
competitors.note: Microcontrollers and analog for industrial and embedded markets.

competitors.name: Renesas Electronics Corporation
competitors.note: Automotive and industrial MCUs plus analog and power after buying Intersil and Dialog.

competitors.name: ON Semiconductor Corporation (onsemi)
competitors.note: Power semiconductors, analog and sensors for automotive and industrial.

competitors.name: Monolithic Power Systems, Inc.
competitors.note: Power management chips, especially for data-center and AI server power.

competitors.name: Silicon Laboratories Inc.
competitors.note: Wireless IoT microcontrollers; being acquired by TI for $7.5B (expected close 1H 2027).

competitors.name: Qualcomm Incorporated
competitors.note: Power management and embedded processing for phones and IoT.

competitors.name: Allegro MicroSystems, Inc.
competitors.note: Magnetic sensors and power ICs for automotive and industrial.

competitors.name: ROHM Co., Ltd.
competitors.note: Analog, power and discrete semiconductors, strong in Japanese automotive.

competitors.name: SG Micro Corp
competitors.note: Chinese analog chip maker competing at the lower end of the Chinese market.

competitors.name: Nexperia (Wingtech)
competitors.note: Standard logic, discretes and some analog parts.

threats: Chinese analog suppliers (SG Micro and others) gaining share in China, TI's largest regional market, helped by local-sourcing policies and tariffs.
Heavy capex (about $50B over six years) and fab depreciation pressuring gross margin and free cash flow if demand weakens again.
Cyclical industrial and automotive demand; revenue fell from $20,028M in 2022 to $15,641M in 2024.
Integration and debt risk from the $7.5B all-cash Silicon Labs acquisition.
Analog Devices, Infineon and Monolithic Power competing hard for fast-growing AI data-center power content.
Trade restrictions and tariffs between the U.S. and China.

ceo.name: Haviv Ilan
ceo.background: Electrical engineer (B.S. and M.S., Tel Aviv University) with a Kellogg/Tel Aviv University executive MBA; joined TI in 1999 and was COO from 2020 to 2023

c1.evidence: TI is the largest analog chip maker, but analog is a mature, cyclical industry; only its data-center segment (about 90% year-over-year growth in Q1 2026) is fast-growing.

c2.evidence: Customers choose TI for its 80,000+ product catalog, dependable owned U.S. 300mm supply and low cost, advantages built over decades that rivals relying on foundries find hard to copy.

c3.evidence: Engineers see TI as the default analog supplier and the public knows its TI-84 calculators, but it is far less of a household name than Google, Amazon or NVIDIA.

c4.evidence: TI's stated passion to 'create a better world by making electronics more affordable through semiconductors' is consistent, but its public messaging is dominated by free-cash-flow-per-share and capital management rather than purpose.

c6.evidence: “calculators, chips, reliable, old-school” — the impression is mostly positive: a dependable, long-established Texas tech company best known to the public for school calculators.

c7.evidence: The analog and embedded market is large and grows with electrification, automation and AI data centers, but it grows in the mid-single digits over a cycle rather than riding a hyper-growth trend.

c8.evidence: Data-center power, robotics and the Silicon Labs wireless deal open new areas, but TI stays within analog and embedded chips rather than entering new industries.

m1.evidence: Haviv Ilan has a clear long-term plan (owned 300mm capacity, dependable supply, data-center power), but it is an operator's strategy rather than a sweeping vision of the future.

m2.evidence: Ilan is not a founder, but TI's stated ambition to 'act like owners who will own the company for decades' and its multi-year fab build-out show long-term thinking.

m4.evidence: There is little public evidence either way on whether Ilan leads in a servant-leadership style.

m5.evidence: TI has a strong, distinctive engineering and manufacturing culture that keeps releasing hundreds of new parts a year, but it was built over decades, mostly before Ilan.

m6.evidence: Ilan holds bachelor's and master's degrees in electrical engineering and ran analog and wireless businesses before becoming CEO.

m7.evidence: There is no notable controversy, but also no clear public evidence of a broader humanitarian mission; he sold 20,000 shares in May 2026 under normal executive selling.

m7b.evidence: No record found of Haviv Ilan giving a commencement speech at a top university.

m8b.evidence: Ilan keeps a low, disciplined public profile with no distinctive celebrity persona.

m9.evidence: Since he became CEO in 2023 revenue fell from $17,519M to $15,641M (2024) before recovering to $17,682M (2025) and 23% growth in Q2 2026, while he delivered the Sherman and Lehi fab ramps.

m10.evidence: TI is known for disciplined cost control, flat R&D-plus-SG&A spending (about $3.9B a year) and returning all free cash flow over time.

c10.evidence: TI chips quietly power cars, medical devices, factories and chargers used by billions of people, but no single product changes lives the way a consumer platform does.

p2.evidence: Making tens of billions of reliable analog chips a year in advanced 300mm fabs is hard, and these chips are essential to almost all electronics.

f2.evidence: Gross margin fell from 64.1% (2020) to 57.0% (2025) and operating margin from 40.8% to 34.1%, mainly from new-fab depreciation.

f3.evidence: At June 30, 2026 debt was $14,052M against $7,001M of cash and short-term investments, but TTM operating cash flow of $8,667M and equity of $18,007M make it manageable.

f4.evidence: Operating income was $5,894M in 2020 and only $6,023M in 2025 after peaking at $10,140M in 2022 and falling in 2023 and 2024, and operating cash flow was $6,139M in 2020 versus $7,153M in 2025, with declines in 2023 and 2024.

v1.evidence: TI is the broadest and most dependable analog supplier, but in many niches parts from Analog Devices or Infineon are just as good or better, so there is no single NVIDIA-like reason to choose it.

v2.evidence: TI is a respected employer but not near the top of major best-workplace rankings; its most recent verified listing was No. 295 on Fortune's 2021 World's Most Admired All-Star list.

c5.evidence: If TI disappeared, carmakers, factory-equipment makers, medical-device makers and data-center builders would face chip shortages, because TI supplies tens of billions of chips a year to more than 100,000 customers.
